body.text: It would be a big mistake to view the Republicans’ midterm cataclysm as being solely about petrol prices. Defeats on this scale — their worst since the midterms after Watergate, with one of the biggest swings in the last century — don’t happen for mundane reasons.

Yes, higher prices mattered, but inflation was much worse in 2022 and the swing against the Democrats that year was far lower. In Associated Press’s Tuesday-night exit poll, 39 per cent of voters cited the economy as the most important issue for them, but 32 per cent chose the state of democracy. That group voted Democrat by 80 per cent to 20 per cent. The issues are, of course, connected. Higher supermarket bills seem more outrageous when the president is banging on about his new golden ballroom or his billion-dollar Qatari jet. For the Democrats, the cost of living and corruption are part of the same message.

We can see that this election was about far more than the economy from the differing performances of candidates. In Texas and Georgia, Trump pushed the nominations of Ken Paxton and Mike Collins, both of whom were embroiled in ethics investigations. Both were hammered, albeit by strong Democratic candidates.

The vicious vulgarity and gleeful ignorance of extreme MAGA were also decisively rejected. In Ohio, the profoundly unpleasant Vivek Ramaswamy underperformed other statewide candidates in losing the gubernatorial race to Amy Acton. His decision to run the most disgusting advert in US electoral history, featuring Acton’s estranged mother who had previously accused her of inventing child sexual abuse, backfired badly. In South Carolina, Kansas, and probably Mississippi (depending on the final few votes), low-quality Republican candidates lost states that stronger candidates might well have held. The high-profile conspiracist Lauren Boebert looks set to lose a House race many prediction sites thought was safe.

Where Republicans did outperform in competitive states, it was typically thanks to candidates seen as more moderate or reasonable, like senator Susan Collins in Maine, who couldn’t hold out against the flood but still beat the average swing. Or Kelly Ayotte and Phil Scott, who held on as governors in the otherwise blue states of New Hampshire and Vermont.

This leads to the question of whether the Republican Party can adapt to this reality. Typically, when parties face a defeat on this scale, a self-preservation instinct kicks in and they moderate. Think of Britain’s Labour Party in the late 1980s or the rhetorical shift by Republicans and British Conservatives towards “compassionate conservatism” in the early 2000s.

But the Republican Party has been taken over by the Trump cult, and he retains popularity with a core vote that will be critical for the next round of primaries. The tension created by this could tear the party apart.

The rational incentive for the Republicans to moderate is obvious. America hasn’t suddenly become a country of liberal socialists. There are plenty of socially conservative, low-tax voters who would be willing to back the party but went Democrat or sat at home on Tuesday because they couldn’t face backing someone like Ken Paxton and disapproved of Trump’s behaviour.

The president’s ideologically obsessive administration actively repelled important voter groups who had moved towards the Republicans in 2024. Most obviously, Hispanic voters shifted twenty-two points in favour of the Democrats in these elections. Some of the biggest swings in the country were in South Texas counties, as well as a few in Kansas, which are majority Hispanic and where ICE has been particularly active. Black voters also turned out in larger numbers than usual for a midterm, helping the Democrats take South Carolina, probably Mississippi, and come very close in Louisiana too.

The South is going to become more Hispanic over the next few cycles. Demographics are not destiny, as we saw in 2024, but any sane centre-right party would acknowledge they needed to stop alienating this group.

Yet moderating requires repudiating Trump and the behaviour of his most fervent supporters. Even as his national power slips away, his control over the party has remained strong. Almost every primary candidate he backed won.

For J.D. Vance, the favourite to be the party’s next presidential nominee, this is a particularly tricky challenge. He has spent all year taking not very subtle steps to try and distance himself from Trump, particularly on the Iran War. He went further yesterday, saying towards the end of a lengthy tweet: “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
Perhaps more surprising was a nod to the ICE problem: “I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance.”

But while Vance is canny enough to see at least some of the problem, breaking with the president carries huge risks. He probably needs Trump’s backing to win, and his own brand is based on “owning the libs” rather than seeming reasonable to a broad coalition. His decision, during the campaign, to back Ramaswamy’s attack ad on Acton was indicative of the problem he has. It is also indicative of his genuine beliefs. He really has bought into the idea of a vast liberal conspiracy to undermine America.

The very limited pool of alternative candidates have similar problems. Marco Rubio was seen as more of a moderate before tying himself to Trump, but that means there is still a lot of suspicion over whether he will be adequately tough on immigration. Trump’s consigliere, Stephen Miller, made his name in Republican politics by destroying a bipartisan immigration bill led by Rubio. Positioning himself as the anti-Trump candidate would probably end Rubio’s chances. After that, the field is very thin — next in the betting come also-rans like Ron DeSantis and Ted Cruz or true-believer cranks like Tucker Carlson.

So, both Vance and Rubio will be engaged in a delicate act of trying to distance themselves from Trump while not incurring his wrath. Their hand may be forced, though, by others in the party. There is increasingly fury about the damage the president is doing, but to date elected officials have been wary about saying anything for fear of being primaried. Only when they are already on their way out have people like senator Thom Tillis been more open about their frustrations. The initial post-midterm calls for moderation have been led by people like John Cornyn, who never got the chance to defend his Senate seat in Texas after Trump backed Paxton.

But now two-thirds of Republican senators are safe until at least two years after Trump has departed the presidency. That does not mean they are all going to start speaking out, but it does give them more room for manoeuvre. Once the flood of investigations the Democrats are planning starts revealing more embarrassing information about the president’s behaviour, the pressure to speak out will grow. At some point, the personal risk of association with Trump will outweigh that of being critical towards him.

There are all sorts of potential flashpoints. If the hapless secretary of war, Pete Hegseth, isn’t sacked, it is highly likely he will be impeached, possibly even before the new Congress sits in January. Quite a few Republican senators would be tempted to vote with the Democrats in the subsequent trial given how important a constituency the military are for them. There will also be desperation to shut down the Iran war, but the Iranians are well aware of that, of course, and will push for maximum concessions. If Trump lashes out again in response, that could lead to pushback from his party. The Democrats will seek to pass all sorts of motions on Iran, Epstein and anything else they can think of to embarrass the Republicans and force division.

It is not hard to imagine the party splitting into factions as a result. One will surely be “continuity MAGA,” arguing that the president was tricked into betraying his promises against “forever wars” by his advisers. This “real MAGA has never been tried” contingent will be supported by a media ecosystem that has developed around Trumpworld and has every incentive to become ever more fervent to generate clicks and engagement. Like a parasite that kills its host, MAGA could be the only thing that survives.

There will also be a faction that seeks to moderate — not by returning to what the Republicans used to be (it’s not going to become Mitt Romney’s party again), but by moving away from the extreme excesses of ICE, the endless culture-war obsessions and the juvenile behaviour of Trump staffers. Even DeSantis, who used culture war issues incessantly to win his campaigns to become Florida governor, is now arguing it’s gone too far.

Vance and Rubio will no doubt try to straddle these factions, but it may become impossible to do so as divisions widen. In addition, both factions’ core argument would rely on blaming the president, either for veering from the righteous path or for never having been on it in the first place. Vance could end up becoming the candidate of group one, and Rubio the candidate of group two, but either choice risks upsetting Trump, who may go in search of another candidate willing to be more loyal. He will not enjoy the idea of being a lame duck.

Ultimately, all that has been holding the party together in recent years is fear of the president, who has no sense of loyalty to the party or any close friendships with senior figures. There are some shared beliefs but no substantive platform: no critical legislation they are trying to pass or economic policy they agree on. That is why they resorted to campaigning on absurd culture war hyperbole. The president has no plan for the next two years. Neither does anyone else. Once the fear subsides, these are classic conditions for civil war.

For the Democrats, this all represents an extraordinary opportunity. If they can win the presidency in two years’ time, they will almost certainly have a trifecta that will allow them to nominate judges and pass budgets. It is even possible, assuming the Mississippi and Alaska seats are added to their total, that they could win a filibuster-proof majority of sixty Senate seats next time, allowing them to pass legislation without any Republican support. There are two very winnable seats up for grabs in Wisconsin and North Carolina, and another four in states they won this time (Kansas, Iowa, South Carolina and Alaska).
The possibility of consolidating their victory in Texas also offers many more paths to the 270 Electoral College votes needed for the presidency, as it accounts for forty of them.

The major risk to this happening is internal party division. These elections did nothing to resolve the growing divide between Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, candidates and the more conservative establishment party leadership. They managed to hold it together during the campaign, but discomfort with new Michigan senator Abdul El-Sayed’s positions goes well beyond last-minute defector Haley Stevens. Israel is an extraordinarily toxic issue for the party, though if Gadi Eisenkot can find a coalition to replace Benjamin Netanyahu that might help.

A big win gives the Democratic leadership a bit more breathing space. They will not be beholden to DSA Representatives in the House or the handful of more left-wing senators. Equally, they won’t have to bargain to keep pseudo-Republican Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman on board. But they will still be under pressure, particularly Chuck Schumer, their leader in the Senate. Five members of the new Senate intake ran on an explicit pledge not to support him (including El-Sayed and two other more progressive winners — Juliana Stratton in Illinois and Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota).

As I said in my earlier article on how a Democrat-controlled Congress could take shape, Schumer and House leader Hakeem Jeffries will face expectations to be more aggressive towards Trump than they would naturally be, partly because of direct lobbying from their colleagues but also because they will be hoping to forestall a serious DSA presidential run. The obvious candidate for this is Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and if she turned into a serious contender during the primaries, it could make the 2016 Hillary Clinton vs Bernie Sanders battle look like a polite disagreement.

The likely shape of the primary contest will form over the next year, and there is a much wider potential field than is available to the Republicans. Kamala Harris is considering another run, as are the soon-to-be former California governor Gavin Newsom and Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro, who again won a swing state with a huge majority. But these midterms have propelled Jon Ossoff into the favourite spot (I hope some readers backed him earlier in the year when I tipped him as one to watch). Having held his Georgia Senate seat by eighteen points in a race that was supposed to be close, he is an obvious choice. Apart from anything else, he would be the youngest-ever president, which would be a blessed relief after the senility of the past decade.

At the moment, Ossoff is saying he has no interest in the presidency and will serve his full term, whereas his Georgia Senate colleague, Raphael Warnock, is making noises about running. But there will be a lot of pressure for him to stand, given he has an Obama-esque ability to appeal across the Democratic coalition.

No doubt there will be numerous differences of opinion amongst the Democrats in the run-up to the presidential election. But if they can find a unifying candidate, they should be able to avoid a major split. The size of the opportunity and the collective desire to defeat a party they see as an existential threat to democracy should be enough motivation. Their problems will come once they are in power.

The Republicans, though, are going to suffer a miserable few years as a consequence of allowing Trump to take over their party. They are now in hock to the whims of a decrepit, vengeful narcissist with no interest in the party’s future. Their talent pool is badly diminished, with staffer jobs in the Trump administration dominated by deeply unappealing online edgelords. They have no obvious saviour.

If it weren’t for the inflexible design of the American two-party system, one would wonder about their long-term survival. Unlike in Europe, it is not possible for a centre-right and radical right party to coexist. This means the battle for control must be fought within the party, with no guarantee of a resolution or of the right side winning.

The most likely outcome for the near future is no dramatic repudiation of MAGA but a muddle of ideologically incoherent competing factions, all trying to find a pathway to electability while keeping Trump’s supporters in the tent. They could be lost in the wilderness for a long time. •
